newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-CORRETJA FIRST FINALIST AT ITALIAN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CORRETJA FIRST FINALIST AT ITALIAN OPEN.

text.p: Spaniard Alex Corretja reached his fourth clay court final of the season at the Italian Open in Rome on Saturday, aided by an erratic performance from Goran Ivanisevic.
The 10th seeded Spaniard's clay court skills were simply too consistent for the Croatian world number six, whose nerve failed him at the crucial stages of a 7-6 (7-5) 7-6 (7-4) defeat.

Ivanisevic, bidding for his second Rome final - he lost in 1993 to American Jim Courier - dropped his serve when serving for the first set, missed a set point in the second on the Corretja serve at 5-4 and letting slip a mini-break in the tie-break.

On Sunday Corretja, finalist in Munich and Monte Carlo but a winner only at Estoril, will now play the winner of the other semi-final between Chilean seventh seed Marcelo Rios and unseeded Spaniard Alberto Berasategui.
Corretja attributes his reputation as the most consistent player on clay going into the French Open, which starts on Monday week, to a decision to bring back childhood coach Javier Duarte.
"Now my game is more aggressive. I used to have fear of going to the net. Now if I go, I go," he said.
But despite winning 21 matches on clay and reaching four finals, Corretja said that his world number 15 ranking made him an also-ran among Spain's growing school of clay court specialists.
"In Spain, I'm not that good because the people just know the top 10 so you have to do it better every week," he said.
"Even in Barcelona nobody knows me."
Ivanisevic, bidding for his second Rome final since defeat to American Jim Courier in 1993, broke Corretja in the very first game of the match, and held serve to 5-4.
But having shellshocked Corretja with what the Spaniard later called "missile" serves of over 200 kph, Ivanisevic failed to get a single first serve in, and a relieved Corretja levelled at 5-5.
Suddenly, the air of calm that has filled Ivanisevic's game since returning here from a five-week absence with a factured finger vanished.
Yells of anger and frustration started to accompany unforced errors as Ivanisevic self-destructed in the tiebreak.
Both players held serve to 5-4 for Corretja when the Croat cracked.
Inexplicably, choosing to stay back and rally with a man whose ground strokes are the strongest part of his game, Ivanisevic dropped his serve by hitting a backhand long.
A powerful first serve saved the first set point but another unforced error - a forehand into the net - handed Corretja a first set he had looked certain to lose.
Ivanisevic's inner turmoil was betrayed at the start of the second by an extraordinary shot at 15-40 on Corretja's serve with two break points in his favour.
With the court at his mercy, the Croatian leapt into the air to play a routine backhand and blasted the ball out of the Foro Italico.
"I make jump which was pretty stupid wanting to look good, but instead I look bad," said Ivanisevic.
When his next shot landed in the net, Ivanisevic slammed his racket onto the court.
The Croat regained his concentration to hold serve to 6-5 and earn himself a set point on the Corretja serve. But again he let himself be drawn into a long baseline rally, netting a backhand.
In the tiebreak, Ivanisevic finally came into the net to claim a mini-break with a double volley but promptly lost it. Corretja moved to 6-3 with a forehand pass and took the tie-break 7-4.
